- $f:R\to R$ defined by $f(x)=x+1$
- $g:Q\to R$ defined by $g(x)={x}^{2}$
- $h:Z\to Q$ defined by $h(x)={2}^{x}$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a function $f:X\to Y$ is a bijection if it is both a surjection and an injection.

- I is a bijection. First of all, it is a surjection because $∀\,y\in R,$ we can choose an $x\in R$ such that $f(x)=y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =y \\ x+1 & =y \\ x & =y-1\in R\end{aligned}
$$

We verify that, 

$$
f(x)=f(y-1)=(y-1)+1=y.
$$

Second, it is an injection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}f({x}_{1}) & =f({x}_{2}) \\ {x}_{1}+1 & ={x}_{2}+1 \\ {x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f$ is both surjective and injective, $f$ is bijective.    

- II is *not* a bijection because it is not surjective. As a counterexample, choose $y=2.$ Then there is no rational number $x$  such that $g(x)=2.$ The only numbers $x$ that satisfies ${x}^{2}=2$ are $x=\pm \sqrt{2}\notin Q.$

- III is *not* a bijection because it is not surjective. As a counterexample, choose $y=0.$ Then there is no integer $x$  such that $g(x)=0,$  because ${2}^{x}>0$ for all $x\in Z.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-26c1f05c-d5ac-55f3-a9f9-404f5c918451"] :db/ensure $$
-\frac{\pi }{2}<\operatorname{arctan}⁡x<\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, for example, there is no value $x\in R$ such that $f(x)=4.$

- II is a bijection. First of all, it is a surjection because $∀\,y\in R,$ we can choose an $x\in R$ such that $g(x)=y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =y \\ 2x & =y \\ x & =\frac{y}{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

We verify that

$$
g(x)=g(\frac{y}{2})=2(\frac{y}{2})=y.
$$

Second, it is an injection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}g({x}_{1}) & =g({x}_{2}) \\ 2{x}_{1} & =2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $g$ is both surjective and injective, $g$ is bijective.

- III is *not* a bijection because it is not surjective. Notice that if $x$ is an integer number, then $h(x)=2x$ is an even number. This means that the range of $h$ is the set of even numbers.
So, for example, there is no value $x\in Z$ such that $h(x)=3.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b94f51c3-8089-500c-bb22-065f6d87882e"] :db/ensure - I is *not* a bijection because it is not surjective. Remember that the range of $\operatorname{arctan}⁡x$ is $(-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}).$ This means that 

$$
-\frac{\pi }{2}<\operatorname{arctan}⁡x<\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, for example, there is no value $x\in R$ such that $f(x)=4.$

- II is a bijection. First of all, it is a surjection because $∀\,y\in R,$ we can choose an $x\in R$ such that $g(x)=y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =y \\ 2x & =y \\ x & =\frac{y}{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

We verify that

$$
g(x)=g(\frac{y}{2})=2(\frac{y}{2})=y.
$$

Second, it is an injection: 

$$
\begin{aligned}g({x}_{1}) & =g({x}_{2}) \\ 2{x}_{1} & =2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}\end{aligned}

- the outputs of the function cover the entire range, and
- every output comes from a unique input (no two inputs map to the same output).

This course serves as ideal preparation for students wishing to pursue undergraduate studies in formal mathematical disciplines, including Discrete Mathematics, Abstract Algebra, and Real Analysis.

A robust knowledge of set theory is another cornerstone of mathematical proof-writing. Students will extend and formalize their understanding of sets and learn to translate between logical and set operations. By the end of the course, students will appreciate how set theory provides a comprehensive toolkit for proving mathematical results.
After mastering these fundamentals, students will explore various proof-writing techniques, including direct proof, proof by cases, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, disproof, and mathematical induction. The course emphasizes proving concepts related to parity, divisibility, congruence, sequences, functions, set identities, and relations. Students will have multiple opportunities to test and refine their proof construction and comprehension skills throughout the course and in varied contexts
